primary_cause: Expected COVID-related production shutdowns and collapsing auto demand. By Mar 18 GM Ford FCA said would suspend North American manufacturing through at least Mar 30. UAW pressure
secondary_factors: March 16 market crash still reverberating. Investors pricing in recession and supply-chain disruption across cyclicals
store_description: GM March 17 decline looks mostly tied to the market discounting an imminent North American production halt. That expectation was validated the next day when GM confirmed an orderly suspension of manufacturing through at least March 30.

primary_cause: No material NextEra-specific negative. Mar 18 cash-crunch selloff — even Treasuries sold. Utility-sector de-risking during liquidity panic
secondary_factors: Falling power-demand expectations from recession fears. Indiscriminate selling of defensive yield names as investors raised cash
store_description: For NEE no strong stock-specific trigger. The most plausible explanation is that utilities sold off with other bond-proxy and defensive names as investors dumped liquid assets for cash even sending Treasury yields sharply higher on March 18.

primary_cause: Expected hit to smartphone and consumer-electronics memory demand from COVID plus semiconductor cyclicality. Mar 25 commentary said COVID would hurt smartphone and consumer-electronics demand but data-center improving
secondary_factors: General tech and semiconductor liquidation. Fears over supply-chain disruption
store_description: MU drop looks less like a one-off Micron event and more like investors aggressively repricing memory demand. Reuters later quantified the core issue: coronavirus was expected to hurt smartphone and consumer-electronics sales while Micron tried to offset by redirecting supply toward data-center.

primary_cause: Ongoing repricing of Microsoft coronavirus supply-chain and PC-hardware exposure. Already warned Feb 26-27 coronavirus would cause Windows and Surface to miss prior guidance. Supply chain recovering more slowly than expected
secondary_factors: March 18 liquidity-driven tech selling. Recession fears
store_description: MSFT March 18 move was not just generic market pain. Investors were still digesting Microsoft late-February warning that its More Personal Computing segment especially Windows OEM and Surface would miss guidance because Chinese production normalization was slower than expected.

primary_cause: No Morgan Stanley-specific negative. Severe market stress scramble for cash. Mar 18 investors even sold Treasuries. Financial-sector stress tied to liquidity funding and recession fears
secondary_factors: Exposure to trading underwriting and credit-market dislocation across Wall Street banks
store_description: MS looks mainly macro and sector driven. With markets in a liquidity panic investors hit brokers and banks on fears that violently widening spreads funding pressure and recession would overwhelm any benefit from higher trading activity.

primary_cause: No material Merck-specific negative. Broad-market de-risking and healthcare rotation. Investors raising cash across even relatively defensive pharmaceutical names
secondary_factors: None clearly stock-specific in that window
store_description: MRK decline appears to have come despite a lack of fresh company-specific bad news. On March 18 investors were indiscriminately selling liquid large caps across sectors to raise cash which dragged down even defensive pharma names.

primary_cause: No fresh Altria-specific negative. Later results suggested cigarette stockpiling ahead of lockdowns actually helped near-term sales. General market liquidation
secondary_factors: Defensive sectors being sold for cash. MO also carried pre-existing overhangs from JUUL and regulatory concerns
store_description: MO drop looks mostly technical and macro. No obvious new company shock in the immediate window and later evidence that lockdown stockpiling supported tobacco sales suggests the March 18 decline was more about indiscriminate selling.

primary_cause: Investors pricing broad med-tech disruption especially elective-procedure weakness despite positive ventilator headlines. Medtronic said Mar 18 had already increased ventilator production by 40%+ and on track to more than double capacity
secondary_factors: March 18 marketwide liquidation. Positive ventilator headline underscored how deeply COVID disrupting normal med-tech demand
store_description: MDT fell even though its COVID-facing ventilator business was ramping fast with production up more than 40% and capacity set to more than double. The more likely interpretation is that the market focused on the much larger negative read-through for elective procedures.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. McDonald's and Starbucks said closing dine-in areas at many U.S. stores shifting to takeout drive-thru and delivery. Multiple states ordering restaurant dining rooms closed
secondary_factors: State-level restaurant shutdown orders. Recession fears. COVID dining-room closures and traffic collapse risk
store_description: MCD had a real company-specific catalyst: it effectively shut dine-in across much of the U.S. and moved to off-premise service only. Investors were repricing a sudden hit to high-margin in-store traffic just as multiple states were ordering restaurant dining rooms closed.

primary_cause: No fresh Linde-specific negative. Later said crisis would hamper performance further in 2020. Recession-driven concern over industrial gas volumes
secondary_factors: Liquidation of industrials during March 18 cash squeeze
store_description: LIN decline looks like a read-through from the sudden collapse in industrial activity rather than a new company-specific event. Later Reuters coverage confirmed volumes were falling because of the coronavirus crisis.

primary_cause: No material ServiceNow-specific negative. Broad software multiple compression during liquidity panic
secondary_factors: Concern enterprise IT spending would freeze in sudden recession
store_description: For NOW no compelling company-specific catalyst in the lookback window. The most likely explanation is that investors were de-risking high-multiple enterprise software names on fears that CIO budgets and deal cycles would stall.

primary_cause: No Mastercard-specific Mar 15-18 announcement. Business highly exposed to travel-linked cross-border volume. Collapse in travel and cross-border card spending expectations
secondary_factors: General consumer-spending recession fears
store_description: MA decline was most likely a payments-specific read-through from the sudden stop in travel. Investors were quickly repricing a sharp drop in high-margin cross-border transaction volumes as borders tightened and restaurant lodging and travel activity froze.

primary_cause: No discrete Lam-specific negative. Severe semiconductor-equipment selloff. Fears of handset demand collapse supply-chain disruption and capex risk
secondary_factors: High-beta tech liquidation on March 18
store_description: LRCX 15.3% drop looks mostly sector driven but in a stock-specific way: investors were repricing the whole wafer-fab-equipment chain for a sudden global electronics downturn.

primary_cause: Lowe's remained open as essential retailer but cut store hours. Retail operational disruption. Fear non-essential categories would be crushed despite stores staying open
secondary_factors: Broad retail selloff. Recession fears. Reduced hours traffic disruption risk that discretionary big-ticket projects would stall
store_description: LOW decline came even though home improvement stores generally avoided immediate forced closure. The market was still pricing major operational friction reduced hours traffic disruption and the risk that discretionary big-ticket projects would stall.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC context. Already said late January coronavirus would hurt Q1 sales. Reuters: plants in China operating below capacity transportation costs rising from truck shortages
secondary_factors: March 18 consumer-staples de-risking. Global recession fears. Existing coronavirus pressure on sales plant utilization and logistics
store_description: MDLZ had a genuine company-specific COVID overhang. Investors already knew from January that the outbreak was hurting first-quarter sales while factories in China were running under capacity and transport costs were rising.

primary_cause: No fresh Nvidia-specific negative. Later commentary emphasized data-center and gaming demand held up relatively well. Broad semiconductor and tech liquidation
secondary_factors: Fears over PC gaming and supply-chain demand visibility in sudden recession
store_description: NVDA decline appears mostly to have been a beta-driven chip selloff. No strong stock-specific negative headline in the lookback window and later evidence that pandemic conditions actually supported gaming and data-center demand makes the March 18 drop look more like temporary derisking.

primary_cause: Anticipated collapse in freight volumes as economy shut down. Later withdrew 2020 volume and operating-ratio forecasts. Business shutdowns crushing shipment volumes
secondary_factors: Industrial and transport-stock liquidation during cash squeeze
store_description: UNP 10.5% slide is best explained by the market front-running a steep drop in rail volumes. That concern proved correct when the railroad later withdrew its 2020 guidance after volumes fell 7% in the quarter.

primary_cause: No major Philip Morris-specific negative. More exposed than Altria to disrupted global distribution FX and cross-border lockdown effects. Reuters later showed pandemic rules could suspend tobacco manufacturing
secondary_factors: Dollar strength. EM exposure. Indiscriminate selling. Global lockdown and distribution risk hitting internationally exposed tobacco name
store_description: PM outsized drop versus MO likely reflects its more global footprint rather than a single headline. With countries imposing fast-changing restrictions and parts of the tobacco supply chain facing operational suspensions investors seem to have treated PMI as a global-disruption proxy.

primary_cause: Smartphone-demand and handset-supply disruption from COVID. Already warned Mar 2 China virus threatened phone-industry disruption. Kept 2020 5G handset estimate at 175M-225M
secondary_factors: Semiconductor selloff. Doubts about near-term 5G adoption timing. Later Reuters coverage made clear near-term smartphone demand and supply being hit
store_description: QCOM had a clear stock-specific overhang: management had already flagged virus-driven disruption to the phone industry. By March 18 the market was aggressively pricing the risk that collapsing handset demand and supply bottlenecks would overwhelm the longer-term 5G story.

primary_cause: Commercial aerospace collapse tied to sudden stop in air travel. No fresh Raytheon/UTC merger-specific negative. Flights canceled borders tightened travel collapsed
secondary_factors: Merger-complexity uncertainty. Broad industrial liquidation. Investors aggressively repriced jet-engine avionics and aftermarket exposure
store_description: RTX 14.5% decline looks primarily like a commercial-aerospace shock not a discrete corporate event. As travel restrictions and shutdowns spread investors aggressively repriced jet-engine avionics and aftermarket exposure swamping the more defensive defense side.
